}}'''Eugene John "Gene" Mele''' is a professor of [[physics]] at the [[University of Pennsylvania]], where he researches quantum electric phenomena in condensed matter.<ref name="Penn">{{cite web | title=Eugene Mele | website=www.physics.upenn.edu | url=https://www.physics.upenn.edu/people/standing-faculty/eugene-mele | access-date=20 October 2018}}</ref> He is known for predicting the [[quantum spin Hall effect]].

==Biography==

Mele graduated from [[Saint Joseph's University]] in 1972 and obtained a Ph.D. in physics from the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] in 1978. After working as a research assistant at the [[Xerox]] Research Center in [[Webster, New York]], he was appointed assistant professor at the University of Pennsylvania in 1981 and promoted to full professor in 1989. Since 2014 he has also been visiting faculty at [[Loughborough University]] in the United Kingdom.

==Research==

Together with [[Charles L. Kane|Charles Kane]], he predicted the [[quantum spin Hall effect]] in graphene which later was called time-reversal invariant [[topological insulator]] for the corresponding two dimensional structures.<ref>{{cite journal|first1=C.L. |last1=Kane |first2=E.J. |last2=Mele |title=Quantum Spin Hall Effect in Graphene |journal=Physical Review Letters |volume=95 |issue=22 |pages=226081 |date=25 November 2005 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.95.226801|pmid=16384250 |arxiv=cond-mat/0411737 |bibcode=2005PhRvL..95v6801K |s2cid=6080059 }}</ref> The existence of [[quantum spin Hall effect]] has since been experimentally verified in HgTe quantum wells, and the prospect of applications for these old materials (predicted by others) has stimulated new research interest.{{sfnp|Kane|Moore|2011}}

==Honours and awards==

Mele and Kane were awarded the 2019 [[Breakthrough Prize in Fundamental Physics]].<ref name="BPFF">{{cite web | title=Breakthrough Prize – Winners of the 2019 Breakthrough Prize in Life Sciences, Fundamental Physics and Mathematics Announced | website=Breakthrough Prize | date=17 October 2018 | url=https://breakthroughprize.org/News/47 | access-date=20 October 2018}}</ref> and the 2018 [[BBVA Foundation Frontiers of Knowledge Award]] in Basic Sciences. They had previously received the [[Benjamin Franklin Medal (Franklin Institute)|Benjamin Franklin Medal]] of the [[Franklin Institute]] in 2015, with [[Shoucheng Zhang]],<ref name="Franklin">{{cite web | title=Eugene J. Mele | website=The Franklin Institute | date=27 October 2014 | url=https://www.fi.edu/laureates/eugene-j-mele | access-date=20 October 2018}}</ref> and the [[European Physical Society]] Condensed Matter Division Europhysics Prize in 2010 with Zhang, [[Hartmut Buhmann]], and [[Laurens W. Molenkamp|Laurens Molenkamp]].<ref>{{cite web| url=http://c.ymcdn.com/sites/www.eps.org/resource/collection/E5F070A4-808E-4FD3-9217-06F321ED3CE1/EPS_Europhysics_Recipients.pdf| title=EPS Condensed Matter Division Europhysics Prize - Award recipients| publisher=European Physical Society| date=28 September 2017| access-date=20 October 2018}}</ref> He was elected a fellow of the [[American Physical Society]] in 2001.<ref> {{cite web|url=https://www.aps.org/programs/honors/fellowships/archive-all.cfm?initial=&year=2001&unit_id=&institution=|title=APS Fellow archive|publisher=APS|access-date= 20 September 2020}} </ref> He was elected to The National Academy of Sciences in 2019.
